_about: Real club histories for Germany, as of the end of the 2024/25 season. Keys are the in-game club names. Written in our own words; check and correct freely.

München Rot.history: Founded by members of a Munich gymnastics club, the club joined the Bundesliga in 1965 and soon dominated, winning three straight European Cups in the 1970s. It has been the leading force in German football ever since, including a run of eleven consecutive titles from 2013 to 2023, and regained the title in 2025.
best: Three European Cups in a row, 1974-76

Dortmund Borussen.history: Formed by young men breaking away from a church youth group, the club became the first German side to win a European trophy in 1966. After near financial collapse in the mid-2000s it rebuilt into a title winner again in 2011 and 2012, and is famed for the huge standing terrace known as the Yellow Wall.

Leverkusen Werkself.history: Created as the works club of the Bayer chemical company, the club reached the top flight in 1979 and won the UEFA Cup in 1988. Long mocked for near misses, it finally broke through in 2023/24 by winning the league unbeaten and adding the cup.

Leipzig Rasenball.history: Set up with backing from Red Bull after taking over a fifth-tier licence, the club climbed four divisions in seven years to reach the Bundesliga in 2016. It quickly became a regular Champions League participant and won back-to-back German cups.

Frankfurt Adler.history: A founding member of the Bundesliga, the club had already won the national title in 1959 and reached the 1960 European Cup final. It has a strong cup tradition and celebrated a famous Europa League triumph in Seville in 2022.

Stuttgart Schwaben.history: One of the most decorated clubs in the south-west, it won two titles in the early 1950s and three more in the Bundesliga era, the latest in 2007. After two relegations it returned strongly, finishing second in 2024 and lifting the German cup in 2025.

Freiburg Breisgauer.history: A modest club from the edge of the Black Forest, it first reached the Bundesliga in 1993 and became known for stable leadership and long-serving coaches. It has become an established top-flight side, regularly qualifying for Europe in recent seasons.

Wolfsburg Wölfe.history: Formed in the town built around the Volkswagen factory, the club reached the Bundesliga in 1997 and has stayed there since. Backed by the carmaker, it won a surprise league title in 2009 and followed it with the cup in 2015.

Gladbach Fohlen.history: Under coach Hennes Weisweiler a young, attacking side earned the nickname Foals and dominated the 1970s alongside Bayern. The club won five titles in that decade and reached the 1977 European Cup final.

Hoffenheim Kraichgauer.history: A village club from the Kraichgau, it was transformed by investment from software billionaire and former player Dietmar Hopp. It rose from the lower leagues to the Bundesliga in 2008 and reached the Champions League group stage in 2018/19.
best: Rise from amateur football to the Bundesliga

Mainz Nullfünfer.history: Long a second-division club, it first reached the Bundesliga in 2004 under Jürgen Klopp, later coached by Thomas Tuchel. It has been a top-flight fixture for most of the time since and finished sixth in 2024/25 to return to Europe.

Berlin Eiserne.history: Based in Köpenick, the club was seen as an underdog in East German football and is famous for fans who rebuilt its stadium themselves. It reached the Bundesliga in 2019 and rose to the Champions League group stage in 2023/24.

Bremen Grün-Weiß.history: A Bundesliga founder member, the club enjoyed its best era under Otto Rehhagel in the late 1980s and early 1990s, including European success in 1992. It won a league and cup double in 2004 and returned to the top flight in 2022 after one season down.

Augsburg Fuggerstädter.history: The club spent decades in the lower leagues before winning promotion to the Bundesliga in 2011. It has stayed in the top flight ever since and reached the Europa League round of 32 in 2015/16.

Köln Geißböcke.history: Formed by a merger after the Second World War, the club became the first Bundesliga champion in 1964 and won a double in 1978. It has yo-yoed between divisions in recent decades and won the 2. Bundesliga again in 2024/25.

Hamburg Rothosen.history: The club was the only side to have played every Bundesliga season until its first relegation in 2018. Its peak came under Ernst Happel, winning the European Cup in 1983, and after seven seasons in the second tier it won promotion back in 2024/25.

Hamburg Kiezkicker.history: Rooted in Hamburg's harbour and nightlife district, the club is known worldwide for its left-leaning fan culture and skull-and-crossbones symbol. Mostly a second-tier side, it won the 2. Bundesliga in 2024 and stayed up in its 2024/25 return to the top flight.
best: Beat Bayern in 2002 as reigning world club champions

Heidenheim Brenzer.history: The football section split from the town's old sports club (dating to 1846) in 2007, with coach Frank Schmidt in charge from that year. It climbed from regional amateur football to the Bundesliga in 2023, reached the Conference League knockout play-offs in 2024/25 and survived relegation via play-off.
best: Eighth in its first Bundesliga season

Gelsenkirchen Knappen.history: A club of the Ruhr mining community, it dominated German football in the 1930s and 1940s with its short-passing style. It won the UEFA Cup in 1997 and was a regular title challenger, but has spent recent seasons in the second division after relegation in 2023.

Berlin Alte Dame.history: The capital's biggest club won back-to-back national titles in 1930 and 1931 and plays at the Olympiastadion. It reached the Champions League second group stage in 1999/2000 but has yo-yoed since, dropping to the second tier again in 2023.

Hannover Roten.history: Champions of Germany in 1938 and 1954, the club made history in 1992 by winning the DFB-Pokal as a second-division side. It reached the Europa League quarter-finals in 2012 and has played in the 2. Bundesliga since 2019.
best: DFB-Pokal winners 1992 as a second-tier club

other: Eight titles before the Bundesliga (1920-1961), ninth in 1968

Nürnberg Club.history: The dominant German club of the 1920s, it held the record for most national titles for decades. It won its ninth championship in 1968 but was relegated the following season, and has since been a frequent mover between the top two divisions.

Düsseldorf Flingeraner.history: The club won its only national title in 1933 and enjoyed a strong spell around 1980, lifting two straight German cups. It has since moved between the divisions, with Bundesliga spells as recently as 2018-2020.

Kaiserslautern Betze.history: Home club of Fritz Walter and the core of West Germany's 1954 World Cup winners, it plays on the steep Betzenberg hill. In 1998 it became the only side to win the Bundesliga straight after promotion, and later fell as low as the third tier.
best: Bundesliga champions 1998 as a promoted side

other: 1909 title won by predecessor club Phönix Karlsruhe

Karlsruhe Wildpark.history: Formed in 1952 from a merger whose roots go back to the 1890s, the club won consecutive German cups in the mid-1950s. Its best modern run came in 1993/94, reaching the UEFA Cup semi-finals after a famous 7-0 win over Valencia.

Paderborn Ostwestfalen.history: The club in its current form came from a 1985 merger, with roots going back to 1907. It reached the Bundesliga for the first time in 2014 and briefly topped the table, and returned for a second top-flight season in 2019/20.
best: Briefly top of the Bundesliga in 2014

Darmstadt Lilien.history: A small Hesse club with short Bundesliga spells around 1980, it made a remarkable rise from the third tier to the top flight in 2015. It returned to the Bundesliga again in 2023/24 but went straight back down.

Bochum Blau-Weiß.history: Tracing its roots to a 19th-century gymnastics club, it spent 1971 to 1993 in the Bundesliga without relegation, earning the nickname 'the unrelegatable'. It qualified for the UEFA Cup twice and was relegated from the top flight again in 2024/25.

Kiel Störche.history: Germany's northernmost professional club won the national title in 1912 but then waited over a century for top-flight football. It finally reached the Bundesliga for 2024/25 and was relegated after one season.

Magdeburg Elbkicker.history: One of East Germany's strongest sides, the club won three league titles and became the only DDR team to lift a European trophy, beating AC Milan in 1974. After reunification it fell to the lower leagues before returning to the 2. Bundesliga.

Fürth Kleeblatt.history: In its early years the club was a major power of German football with three titles. After merging with the football section of TSV Vestenbergsgreuth in 1996 it became a second-tier mainstay, with Bundesliga seasons in 2012/13 and 2021/22.

Braunschweig Löwen.history: A Bundesliga founder member, the club won a surprise championship in 1967. In 1973 it became the first German team to carry a shirt sponsor, and its most recent top-flight season was 2013/14.

Bielefeld Arminen.history: A frequent mover between divisions, the club has had several Bundesliga spells, most recently 2020-2022. After falling to the third tier it won the 3. Liga in 2024/25 and reached the German cup final the same season.
best: DFB-Pokal finalists 2025 as a third-tier side

Dresden SG.history: One of the most successful clubs in East Germany, it won eight DDR titles and seven cups and was a regular in Europe. It played four Bundesliga seasons after reunification and won promotion back to the 2. Bundesliga in 2024/25.

Münster Preußen.history: The club reached the national championship final in 1951 and was a founding member of the Bundesliga in 1963, though it lasted only one season. After decades in the lower leagues it returned to the 2. Bundesliga in 2024 and stayed up.

Elversberg Saarländer.history: From a small community in the Saarland, the club rose with back-to-back promotions to reach the 2. Bundesliga in 2023. In 2024/25 it finished third and came close to the Bundesliga, losing the promotion play-off to Heidenheim.
